rows.en: The men who stood at the head of the Sanhedrin at that time were Shemaiah and Avtalyon. Their origin is not clearly known, but it was said of them that they were of the seed of proselytes. And it is no wonder that they were chosen into the Sanhedrin, even though there was a fixed law that proselytes should not sit in a court; for it is not said that they themselves were proselytes, only that their descent was from proselytes, and who knows how many generations earlier their fathers had become proselytes, had been absorbed among the Jews and had married daughters of Israel; and in this way even one who is of the seed of proselytes can be in the Sanhedrin. Therefore we have no compelling reason not to believe a clear tradition that spread among the Jews, already in ancient days, that these two sages were of the seed of proselytes and applied themselves to the Torah until they attained an honored rank and became the heads of the Sanhedrin.{v1_08_14:1} According to the tradition they received from Simeon ben Shetaḥ and from Judah ben Tabbai. And indeed they were their disciples in Torah and in the fear of sin, but they were not their disciples with respect to their political views. For Simeon and his colleagues not only took part in the affairs of the government; they were nearly its leaders, at any rate during all the nine years in which Shelaminon⚠1 reigned in her widowhood. Not so Shemaiah and Avtalyon. They recognized that they would do more for the survival of the nation if they set their whole aim only on straightening and bringing order into religious matters than if they took part in the affairs of the government. Therefore they made one point alone the goal of their striving, and that was the upholding of the Torah. Toward this goal they united all their strength, and from all affairs of the government they drew back their hand. For they did not close their eyes to how badly the foundations of their political condition were shaken, and that it was beyond human strength to hold them up. The wars and the upheavals had razed to the foundation every hope of returning to the firm ground of their freedom as in former days. Therefore they rightly thought: why should they waste their strength in vain to attain a thing that is far from them, with almost no hope of attaining it because of the many who prevent and hinder it? Is it not better to work for a thing that is near to them, namely the study of the Torah, about which their heart was firm and sure that if they upheld the Torah they too would be upheld, and by keeping it they would give an everlasting safeguard to their nation? And indeed they attained this aim with ease. For the government, wishing to rule as it pleased, also made peace with their aim, and no one disturbed their quiet. The sayings of these sages bear the marks of this idea. Shemaiah used to say (Avot ch. 1): "Love work, hate lordship, and do not make yourself known to the ruling power." With these words he rouses the hearts not to take part in the affairs of the government, nor in the quarrels and wars, which at that time were not conducted for the good of the nation, as in the days of the first Hasmoneans, but for the gain of individuals; that they should try in every possible way to keep far from dominion and from becoming known to the kingdom, but should go in their simplicity, seeking work and occupying themselves with it, and should not set their eyes on attaining lordship and dominion. And Avtalyon warned the sages still more to guard their lips against speaking against the kingdom, saying: "Sages, be careful with your words, lest you incur the penalty of exile and be exiled to a place of evil waters, and the disciples who come after you drink and die, and the name of Heaven be profaned." This moral idea too is taken from experience. And there is no doubt that when he spoke these words he had in mind the many events that had befallen the sages in the generations before him. For time after time many of them went into exile to Alexandria, and the exile was the undoing of the disciples who went into exile with their masters and learned there new views with which the spirit of the Pharisee sages was not at ease. From their desire to keep the peace with the government they strove not to give it pretexts for stirring up jealousy against the Pharisees, as had happened before at various times. To attain this end they saw that it was good to limit the number of the disciples. They knew well that there was not one of all the governments of those days that did not look on the mass of the Pharisees with an evil eye. And in order to put a little restraint on the people, so that many should not break in to enter the house of study, Shemaiah and Avtalyon enacted that whoever wished to be one of those who came to their house of study should pay half a tropaik (which is a ma'ah and a half) to the guard at the door (Yoma 35b). And although on the one hand this enactment was a cause of reducing those who studied, on the other hand it was of great benefit, in that men who were not called, both by their natural capacities and because they had a foreign intention and studied only for some other purpose, did not mingle among them. This effort of theirs gave them confidence that they would not make themselves odious in the eyes of the government, and they could hope to go safely among the storms of the times. And they did not take to heart that by this the learners and students would become fewer, for they knew well that wisdom has never been measured by the number of the men who occupy themselves with it; rather its perfection is attained even if those who seek it are only few, provided these few occupy themselves with it with ability and purity of thought.

From the first time that they were chosen to sit at the head of the Sanhedrin, the wheel of events turned against them, and every day was more dangerous than the one before. In the first days of the rule of John Hyrcanus a thing happened that, at the end of a few days, became a curse for all the sages. After Aristobulus was subdued and the illusory rule passed to John, the remnants of Aristobulus's army gathered, roamed through the land of Galilee and did all kinds of harm to the Syrians and also to the Romans. But Herod, who was governor in the land of Galilee, being a friend and flatterer of the Romans, pursued these remnants with his army and sought them out of their hiding places, until he succeeded in capturing the head of these remnants, called by the name Hezekiah, and with him many of his men. Hezekiah he sentenced to death without inquiry and examination, and all those captured were sentenced to various punishments. Because of this deed wrath went out against Herod from the people and the Sanhedrin. The Sanhedrin took counsel together, and with the consent of Hyrcanus they summoned him to judgment, to give an account of the deed. Herod came before them, but not in the manner fitting for a man under judgment who stands before his judges. Rather, he came clothed in purple and girded with a sword, and around him a great number of his warriors, all armed with swords. The thing displeased the Sanhedrin, but from faintness of heart their arguments were stopped up and they found no words in the trial. Only one among them all knew no fear, and that was Shemaiah. With the zeal for truth and justice that was in him he rebuked his colleagues with hard words for showing partiality in the matter, and he testified against them that they were showing favor in judgment, and he foretold what was to come, saying: the one whom they let go free today against just law will himself be the rod to punish them for it, and he will be their undoing and destroy them. These words of his went down into the chambers of their hearts, their spirit returned to them, and they began to deliberate on the matter. And when Hyrcanus saw that the Sanhedrin was ready to conclude Herod's sentence to death, he ordered them to put off the conclusion of the trial until the next day, and he secretly ordered Herod to save his life and flee from Jerusalem (*Antiquities* 14, 9). Now if from this event we recognize how strong the love of justice was in the heart of Shemaiah, so that he had no fear of any man, it also casts, from another side, a little light on the law of capital cases at that time. First, we see that although Herod did not kill any of those killed with his own hands, but only sentenced them to death and they were killed by his command, the Sanhedrin was nevertheless ready to conclude his sentence to death. It follows that according to the law in force then, the one who sends others to kill a person is liable to death. For only in this way was it possible to hold Herod liable and sentence him to death, although he himself did not kill. And in this deed we find a great connection to the halakhah of Shammai the Elder: "One who says to his fellow, 'Go and kill a person,' the one who sent him is liable" (Kiddushin 43a). And all the fine distinctions of the later authorities and their proofs, which seek to show the opposite by way of midrash and reasoning, none of them equals the proof mentioned, which comes out of a deed that was done. For this deed shows clearly that the halakhah of Shammai the Elder was put into practice in that session of the Sanhedrin, and without doubt it was a decided halakhah. Second, it is fitting for us to consider the argument of the sages against Herod, who said that he had acted against Israelite statute and law, for according to it no one has the right to kill any man, even a sinner, until he has been brought before the Sanhedrin and his sentence to death has been concluded (Josephus, ibid.). And the substance of these words is repeated two and three times in the books of the Oral Torah in the form of a halakhah: "All men are liable if they killed the murderer" (Makkot 12a); "For any murderer, before his sentence to death has been concluded, if a man killed him, he is liable for him as for any other man" (Sifre Mas'ei, section 161). But the sages who lived after capital cases had already been abolished for a long time deliberated on this matter and were divided in their opinions; and both sides of the dispute, both the one whose halakhah agreed with the halakhah that was law in ancient times and was in force in practice, and the one who opposed the ancient halakhah, both of them relied not on tradition but on their own reasoning. For had they paid attention to how the matter was in practice in former times, there would have been no room for a difference of opinion. A third thing comes out of this event: what the masters of the Mishnah set down as a foundation, that all who are liable to death require a warning, and that the sinner must accept death upon himself (Sanhedrin 80b; Tosefta ibid. ch. 10)⚠1, all this had no standing in practice while capital cases were still judged; at any rate such a halakhah was not in force with regard to the death penalty for killing a person. For it is impossible to believe that when Herod sentenced Hezekiah and his companions to death there were witnesses there who had warned him and he had accepted death upon himself and said, "Even so." For how can we believe that at that time there were two men in Galilee who dared to stand up against Herod to warn him, and went unpunished? This rule, that there are many matters which the later authorities derived by their exegesis, which have only the value of a theoretical opinion and never went out into practice, is a great principle for understanding the teachings of our ancients, and here and there we find several examples of this kind. Thus according to the view of the sages of the Mishnah after the destruction, the Sanhedrin carried out the commandment of burning for those liable to burning by means of a wick of lead, which they would light and throw into the mouth of the condemned. But against this R. Eleazar son of R. Zadok mentions an incident that happened with a certain priest's daughter who had committed harlotry, and they surrounded her with bundles of vine branches and burned her; and his colleagues said to him: because the court of that time was not expert (Sanhedrin 52a). Now those sages had no other proof that the burning is by a wick of lead except their midrash, which rests on a gezerah shavah. They had no definite tradition, for if they had said their words from tradition, how could R. Eleazar son of R. Zadok have dared to deny it? Therefore they cast doubt on the expertise of the Sanhedrin and made them a court of Sadducees, for their midrash stood like a wall against that incident. But to which time did R. Eleazar son of R. Zadok testify? Not to the time of Shemaiah and Avtalyon, nor to that of Hillel and Shammai, nor even to the time of Rabban Gamaliel the Elder; for about those times and the Sanhedrin that existed in those times his colleagues could not say that the court of that time was a court of Sadducees. Necessarily, in their view, R. Eleazar son of R. Zadok testified about an early time when there were courts of Sadducees. But R. Eleazar son of R. Zadok tells yet another incident: "I remember when I was a child riding on my father's shoulder, and they brought a priest's daughter who had committed harlotry, surrounded her with bundles of vine branches and burned her." And this he told without doubt about the time of Rabban Gamaliel the Elder; and they said in the baraita that his colleagues answered him that one does not bring a proof from a minor. Thus they saved their midrash and denied the incident that R. Eleazar son of R. Zadok saw with his own eyes. But the more likely thing is that these two incidents are only one, and in truth the commandment of burning was carried out in practice only in the way that R. Eleazar son of R. Zadok told, and the manner of burning as the sages after the destruction decided it was nothing but an exegetical derivation which they drew out by the rule of gezerah shavah, but in practice it was not so. In the same way we find that some sages who lived in the days of the Temple testified about things that they saw with their own eyes, and all this did not prevent other sages from deciding the opposite, and they set aside the testimonies about a deed done in practice with trivial rejections, in order to uphold the derivations of their exegesis which they drew out by their midrash or their reasoning (see Zevaḥim 84a, 103a⚠2; Temurah 18a). From all this, together with matters already mentioned so far here and there, we see that several halakhot that were in force only while the Temple stood were different when they were practiced in fact from how they are described by the later sages; and we will speak of this further below (ch. 21).

rows.en: The event mentioned, the affair of Herod and his summons to judgment before the sages, became a stumbling block in the end. For Herod did not forget what the sages had planned to do against him. And when he came to the throne, the first of his deeds was to persecute the members of the Sanhedrin who had sat in judgment over him and sentenced him to death, and many of them he killed (Bava Batra 3a⚠1). Against Shemaiah and Avtalyon he did not lift his hand, for against his will he gave them honor in his heart, and he did not forget that when he fought Antigonus and besieged Jerusalem they had advised the people to hand the city over to him. And Shemaiah in particular he honored with awe, remembering the words he had spoken on the day he stood before the Sanhedrin for trial, when he foretold that Herod would be the rod that would punish them for having shown him favor that day and been afraid of him. For as he had interpreted to them, so it was; therefore he thought and believed that the spirit of the Lord spoke in him, and for this reason he was afraid to touch him (*Antiquities* 15, 1). The courage of their spirit, fearless in speaking against the high, they showed also in another event. Once a high priest (Hyrcanus or Antigonus) went out of the Temple, and all the people walked after him to escort him. Shemaiah and Avtalyon too were walking together on that road, and when the people who were walking after the high priest saw them, they quickly turned away from him and went to greet Shemaiah and Avtalyon and to escort them. This thing aroused the jealousy of the priest, seeing that these sages were more honored in the eyes of the people than he; but he kept silent and only hid his jealousy in his heart. And when the priest came near his house, Shemaiah and Avtalyon hurried to meet him, to greet him and to take leave of him. But he could no longer restrain himself, and when they came near him he said to them: "Let the sons of the gentiles come in peace." Then they answered him calmly but without partiality: "Let the sons of the gentiles come in peace, who do the deeds of Aaron, and let not the son of Aaron come in peace, who does not do the deeds of Aaron" (Yoma 71b). And what are the deeds of Aaron? The pursuit of peace, for this quality was attributed to Aaron from early times (*Avot de-Rabbi Natan* ch. 12), and all who pursue peace were called disciples of Aaron (Avot ch. 1). The halakhot that go by their name are few. And if we consider them we find that in their days the halakhot had already multiplied and grown to a vast sum; for from the form of their halakhot we recognize that they are necessarily built on the foundations of halakhot that preceded them. In the name of Shemaiah and Avtalyon they testified about a wild animal that nested in an orchard, that it requires designation [in advance], and that a free bird must be tied by its wings so that it will not be exchanged for its mother (Beitzah 25a). And this halakhah is founded on several other halakhot. It presupposes the halakhah that trapping is a principal category of labor (Shabbat 73a), that trapping is not included in the labor of preparing food, that muktzeh is forbidden on a festival, that designation on the eve of the festival removes the muktzeh, and several more halakhot of this kind (Beitzah ch. 1, ch. 3). Another halakhah was reported in their name: "An Israelite woman married to a priest who died and left her pregnant, her slaves may not eat terumah because of the share of the fetus, for the fetus disqualifies and does not entitle to eat" (Yevamot 67a). This halakhah too is founded on other halakhot that preceded it, for there is no room for this halakhah unless we have decided that an Israelite woman who brought slaves to her priest husband, they eat terumah (ibid. 66a), and that the fetus inherits (Bava Batra 141b), and that the newborn entitles its mother to eat terumah (Yevamot 67b; Sifra Emor ch. 20⚠2; Niddah 44a and Rashi there). And two weavers testified in their name that three logs of drawn water disqualify the mikveh (Eduyot 1:3), and it is self-evident that a mikveh that is entirely of drawn water is unfit (Sifra Shemini ch. 9; Mikva'ot 2:4 and R. Samson [of Sens] there). In this we have a clear picture of the manner in which the halakhot widened and the branches multiplied from time to time.

footnotes.en: The scholar Graetz, p. 538, wrote that the expression "he spoke to them in Greek wisdom" refers to the diplomatic stratagems that they learned from the Greeks. We must remark on his words: (a) The word la'az fits only speaking in a foreign tongue. (b) Even if we say that the Greek language is one thing and Greek wisdom another, as the Gemara holds in Bava Kamma (83a), still we do not find in the whole Talmud two kinds of Greek wisdom; and if Greek wisdom in this place is the diplomatic art of the Greeks, then Greek wisdom in the other places of the Talmud too can only be explained as diplomacy, and that is impossible, for in Bava Kamma there they speak of teaching Greek wisdom to small children, and one does not teach diplomacy to boys. (c) In the Talmud in Bava Kamma it is shown explicitly that it made no distinction between the Greek wisdom in which the old man spoke and the Greek wisdom that the boys learned in the house of R. Gamaliel. (d) From the baraita itself it is shown that the Greek wisdom in which the old man spoke is the Greek wisdom that they forbade teaching to children, as is clear to one who studies it there. As for the objection that Greek wisdom was forbidden only at a later time, it is no objection; for we have already seen in several places that such enactments were enacted for their hour and for a passing cause, and they grew lax about them when the cause passed. Therefore we should not wonder if we find that they forbade Greek wisdom at a later time, although it had already been forbidden long before (see there in the Tosafot), just as we do not wonder about other decrees and enactments which, though founded in early times, were renewed in the later generations; and of such cases they said, "they forgot them and founded them again," or "they enacted and it was not accepted, and they enacted again and it was accepted." And therefore I have decided according to the plain sense of the baraita that the decree against Greek wisdom was first founded at that time.

In three places it is told that Shemaiah and Avtalyon were of the seed of proselytes (R. Z. Frankel⚠1, in *Darkhei ha-Mishnah*, p. 37, wrote this of Shemaiah alone, and I do not know his source). In Yoma (71b) it is told that the high priest called them "sons of the gentiles." In Eduyot ch. 5 we learn that Akavya ben Mahalalel said about them, concerning their giving the proselyte woman the waters of the suspected wife to drink, "dugma [those like her] gave her to drink"; and the Yerushalmi, Mo'ed Katan 3:1, explains it as "dekhavatah," that is, that they were proselytes like her, and so Maimonides explained it. And in Gittin (57b) it is taught: "Of the descendants of Sennacherib some taught Torah in public. And who are they? Shemaiah and Avtalyon." But Graetz, p. 540, rejects this for two reasons: (a) that if so he should have said "dekhavatehon" [like them, plural] and not "dekhavatah"; (b) surely a proselyte is unfit to judge. The baraita of Gittin he did not mention, without doubt because the words "who are they? Shemaiah and Avtalyon" are not part of the baraita. But the proof from Yoma is surely strong; why did he not rely on it? And his fine point that he should have said "dekhavatehon" is a poor man's fine point, for the meaning of the Yerushalmi is: those who were like her gave her to drink. And so Rashi explained in Berakhot (19a), and it is stated explicitly in the Tosafot there, s.v. dugma, as we have explained. And even granting that there is no proof from there, there is also no proof for the opposite; so why should we push aside the words of the Gemara, which said explicitly, "And who are they? Shemaiah and Avtalyon"? And why should we close our eyes to the baraita in Yoma, which said explicitly that they were sons of proselytes? To this Graetz said that the baraita was adjusted according to the corrupt opinion of those who mistakenly thought they were proselytes, and perhaps originally there was a different reading in the baraita. But I do not understand why we should corrupt an explicit baraita because of a fine point in the Yerushalmi, and why we should say that the opinion that they were proselytes was founded on the Yerushalmi, which said "dekhavatah gave her to drink." Why not say the opposite: that the account in the baraita is true and the words of the Gemara in Gittin are true, and from this was born the explanation that explained the saying of the Mishnah, "dugma gave her to drink"? But Graetz thought that the baraita and the Gemara are corrupt, because it is impossible that they were proselytes, since proselytes are unfit to judge. But this is no proof, as we have written in the text, and it is made quite clear in Yevamot (45b, 102a) and Kiddushin (76b and Rashi there); and we learn in the Sifre that they said to Agrippa, "You are our brother," because his mother was of Israel. And according to the explanation of Rav Hai Gaon in the *Arukh*, entry dgm, one could argue much, for he explained "a likeness of the waters of the suspected wife" and not the actual waters of the suspected wife; rather they frightened her so that she would confess, in the way Solomon said, "Divide the living child" [1 Kings 3:25]. Graetz agreed with this, but I do not understand: if so, why did they excommunicate Akavya ben Mahalalel? Is it not just to use such a stratagem so that the truth may come out? And see Maimonides, who combined the two explanations.
